title: Hukam: living in the order
hook: the order runs through everything; the Granth invites living in tune with it, not fighting it
tomorrow: Haumai: the disease with its own cure

segments.voice: Yesterday, mahala; your line was every guru signs as nanak, one light passed lamp to lamp. Today, the first of the Granth's great themes, one you met on day one of the Japji.

A few minutes before a concert, the players wander in, and the hall fills with a noisy mess of scales and scraps of melody. Then it goes quiet, and one instrument plays a single long note. Violins, cellos, horns, one by one, slide their pitch until it sits right on that note. Nobody is forced to play the same melody; each keeps its own part. But they're all in tune with one note, and that's what lets the music happen. When one violin refuses, you hear it instantly. Sikhs have a word for the note everything is tuned to.
screen: `THE ORCHESTRA TUNES UP.` → `ONE LONG NOTE.` → `EVERY PART, IN TUNE.`

segments.voice: The word is hukam. It came into Punjabi from Arabic and Persian, where it means a command, an order, a ruling. In the Granth it means the divine order running through everything: how the world is made, how it moves, how it holds together. In the very first pauri of the Japji, Guru Nanak asks how the wall of falsehood can fall, and answers: hukam rajaaee chalanaa, Nanak likhiaa naal. Walk in the will of the order; it's written with you. And in Pauri 2: hukmai andar sabh ko, baahar hukam na koe. Everyone is within the order; no one is outside it. So hukam isn't something you choose to join. You're already inside it, like every instrument in the hall. The only question is whether you play in tune, and the Granth's invitation, again and again, is to live in tune with it instead of fighting it. Fighting it looks like rage at a traffic jam, the endless replay of what should have happened, the demand that the world arrange itself around me. Living in tune means doing your part fully, then accepting what comes as part of a larger music. Sikh teachers are careful here. Living in hukam isn't sitting still while wrong is done; the same tradition honors Gurus who stood up against injustice. It's about where the fighting comes from: ego, or the order. And Pauri 2 ends with the key: whoever understands the hukam stops saying I, I, I.
screen: `HUKAM — THE ORDER IN EVERYTHING.` · `HUKAM RAJAAEE CHALANAA.` · `NO ONE IS OUTSIDE IT.` · `IN TUNE, NOT PASSIVE.` · then, large: `IN TUNE.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing today that isn't the way you wanted, the weather, a delay, a noise outside, an ache, and notice where you've been pushing against it: your jaw, your chest, your thoughts. You don't have to like it; just stop arguing with it, and let it be exactly as it is. Breathe out and let your shoulders drop, like an instrument sliding into tune.
Hukam. The divine order running through everything. No one is outside it, and the Granth invites living in tune with it, not fighting it.
Your line: in tune. Your own part, played inside a larger music. Day two hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs speak of accepting events as bhana, the sweet will, while still working hard and standing up for what is right; the daily hukamnama, a hymn read from the Granth each morning, takes its name from the same word, hukam.
